title: How {language} sounds
summary: Sounds that may be new to you, where the stress goes, and how far you can trust the spelling.

overview.title: Writing and sound
overview.body: How far can the writing tell you how a word sounds, and where does the stress go?

surprises.title: Sounds to watch
surprises.body: A few sounds in {language} behave differently from what you might expect.

complete.body: Gef would like to hear you try that out loud.

tones.title: Tones
tones.body: Pitch is part of the word here. Listen to the same sounds with different pitch.

labels.predictability.high: The writing is a reliable guide to sound: learn the rules and you can read almost any word aloud.
labels.predictability.medium: The writing is mostly a guide to sound, but there are silent letters and a few surprises.
labels.predictability.low: The writing is a poor guide to sound: you often can’t tell how a word is said from how it looks.
labels.stress.rule_with_written_accents: Stress follows a simple rule, and a written accent marks every exception.
labels.stress.mostly_penultimate: Most words are stressed on the second-to-last syllable. The stress usually isn’t written.
labels.stress.phrase_final: Stress falls on the last syllable of a phrase, so words don’t carry their own stress the way English words do.
labels.stress.marked_on_every_word: Every word of two or more syllables has its stressed vowel marked, so you always see where the stress goes.
labels.stress.unpredictable: Stress changes from word to word and usually isn’t written, so you learn it with each word.
labels.sound.trill: A rolled r: the tongue taps against the ridge behind your teeth several times.
labels.sound.velar_fricative: A breathy sound from the back of the mouth, like a soft clearing of the throat.
labels.sound.silent_letter: A letter that is written but not pronounced.
labels.sound.b_v_same: Written v, but pronounced like b.
labels.sound.nasal_vowel: The vowel is pronounced through the nose. A tilde, or an n or m after the vowel, marks it, and the n or m isn’t pronounced as a separate consonant.
labels.sound.front_rounded_vowel: Say “ee” with your lips rounded as if for “oo”.
labels.sound.uvular_r: An r made at the back of the throat, a bit like a gentle gargle.
labels.sound.liaison: A final consonant that is normally silent is often pronounced before a vowel, as in “les amis”.
labels.sound.guttural_r: At the start of a word this r is made at the back of the throat, close to an English h (in Brazilian Portuguese).
labels.sound.affricate_before_i: In Brazilian Portuguese, d before i sounds like the “j” in “judge”.
labels.sound.hard_c_before_i: Ch is a hard k sound here, not the “ch” of “church”.
labels.sound.double_consonant: A written double consonant is pronounced longer, and it changes the word.
labels.sound.dental_fricative: The tongue touches the teeth, as in “think” or “this”.
labels.sound.voiced_velar_fricative: Like a very soft g, with the air still flowing.
labels.sound.many_spellings_one_sound: Several spellings share one sound, so the same sound can be written more than one way.
labels.sound.approximant_r: The tongue curls back or bunches up without touching anything.
labels.sound.spelling_varies: The same letters can sound completely different in different words.
labels.q.hear_pick: Listen and pick the word you hear.
labels.q.which_spelling: Which spelling makes the sound in this word?
labels.tonesys.contour: {language} is a tonal language. Each syllable has a pitch pattern ({count} of them), and the same sounds with a different pattern are a different word.
labels.tonesys.register: {language} is a tonal language: each syllable is said at a high or low pitch level, and that changes the word.
labels.tonesys.pitch_accent: {language} uses pitch accent: how the pitch rises and falls on a word helps tell words apart.
labels.stress.rule_by_syllable_weight: Stress follows a rule based on how heavy the syllables are, so you can work out where it falls.
labels.stress.not_applicable: There is no strong word stress to learn here.
labels.sound.pharyngeal_voiced: A tight, humming sound made deep in the throat. English has nothing like it, so go slowly.
labels.sound.pharyngeal_voiceless: A strong, breathy h made deep in the throat, like fogging up a mirror.
labels.sound.emphatic: A heavy version of a sound you know. Pull the back of your tongue down and back, and the vowels nearby turn deeper.
labels.sound.uvular_stop: Like a k, but made much further back in the throat.
labels.sound.gargle_fricative: A gargling sound at the back of the throat, a bit like the French r, with your voice on.
labels.sound.glottal_stop: The little catch in your throat in “uh-oh”. In Arabic it is a full consonant and can start or end a word.
labels.sound.vowel_length: A long vowel is held about twice as long as a short one, and it can change the word.
labels.sound.aspirated_stops: Pinyin p, t and k are said with a puff of air, like “pin”, “tin” and “kin”. Pinyin b, d and g have no puff: say the p of “spin” instead of a b.
labels.sound.retroflex: For zh, ch and sh, curl the tip of your tongue back toward the roof of your mouth. They sound deeper and heavier than English “j”, “ch” and “sh”. Plain s, c and z are made with the tongue forward.
labels.sound.retroflex_r: Pinyin r is made with the tongue curled back and a slight buzz. It sits somewhere between English “r” and the “s” in “measure”.
labels.sound.palatal: Made with the flat of the tongue against the roof of the mouth and the tip down. Pinyin q is like a light “ch”, x is like a light “sh”, and j is q without the puff of air.
labels.sound.back_unrounded_vowel: Say “oh”, then spread your lips as if smiling, without moving your tongue. That is the sound of pinyin e on its own.
labels.sound.tone_contrast: Same letters, different tone. The tone changes the word.
labels.tone.high_level: High and level. Hold the pitch steady, like singing one note.
labels.tone.rising: Starts in the middle and rises, like asking “what?” in surprise.
labels.tone.dipping: Dips low, then rises a little. In fast speech you often hear only the low dip.
labels.tone.falling: Starts high and drops sharply, like a firm “No!”.
labels.tone.neutral: A short, light syllable with no tone of its own. Its pitch depends on the tone before it.
labels.sound.prenasalized_stop: A quick “m” or “n” that flows straight into the next sound, even at the start of a word, with no vowel in between. Say mb, nd, ng and nj as single sounds.
labels.sound.initial_ng: The “ng” of “sing”, but at the start of a word. Written ng' (with the apostrophe), it is one sound, not n plus g.
labels.sound.tapped_r: A quick tap of the tongue tip behind your top teeth, like the middle of American “butter”. Some speakers roll it.
labels.stress.mostly_final: Most words are stressed on the last syllable.
labels.stress.fixed_initial: The stress is always on the first syllable, so you never have to guess.
